PASSO 1: em português, quando falamos do: STEP 1: English already does something special after "when" with a future meaning: it uses the present, never "will": "When you ARRIVE, call me", not "when you will arrive". Spanish also refuses the future here, but it uses the present SUBJUNCTIVE: «Cuando llegues, llámame», «En cuanto termine» (as soon as I finish), «Hasta que vuelva» (until he comes back). STEP 2: so «cuando llegarás» is wrong, and so is «cuando llegas mañana» (copying English "when you arrive tomorrow"). STEP 3: the general rule: if the action has already happened or is a habit, use the indicative: «Cuando llego a casa, ceno» (habit: whenever I get home), «Cuando llegué, llovía» (past). If the action is in the future and hasn't happened yet, use the subjunctive: «Cuando llegue a casa, cenaré». STEP 4: the clue is in the main clause: if it's in the future, a command or «ir a» + infinitive, the «cuando» clause is usually subjunctive: «Cuando termines, llámame», «Voy a descansar en cuanto acabe». STEP 5: the time conjunctions that follow this rule: «cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que, después de que, mientras (que), una vez que». STEP 6: «antes de que» (before) is special: since the action hasn't happened yet by definition, it ALWAYS takes the subjunctive: «Llámame antes de que salgas» (Call me before you leave). STEP 7: with the same subject, use the infinitive after «antes de» and «después de» — English "before leaving", "after eating": «Llámame antes de salir», «Hablamos después de comer». STEP 8: «mientras» meaning "while (this happens)" takes the indicative: «Mientras cocino, escucho música». About the future, meaning "as long as", it takes the subjunctive: «Mientras no llueva, iremos al parque» (As long as it doesn't rain, we'll go to the park).

For habits and the past, the indicative stays: «Cuando llego a casa, ceno».

PASSO 1: para dizer a finalidade de uma: STEP 1: to say why you do something, Spanish uses «para» (English "to", "in order to"). If the subject is the same in both parts, the next verb stays in the infinitive: «Estudio para aprobar» (I study to pass). STEP 2: if the subjects are different, use «para que» and the subjunctive: «Te lo explico para que lo entiendas» (I'm explaining it so that you understand / for you to understand). English "for you to understand" can't be copied — Spanish has no "for + person + to". STEP 3: the more formal version is «a fin de que» or «con el fin de que»: «Enviamos el aviso a fin de que todos lo lean». STEP 4: «de modo que» and «de manera que» have two uses. Meaning purpose ("so that"), they take the subjunctive: «Habla despacio, de modo que todos lo entiendan». Meaning result ("so, therefore"), they take the indicative: «Habla despacio, de modo que todos lo entienden». English "so that" has the same double meaning. STEP 5: «sin que» always takes the subjunctive: «Sale sin que nadie lo vea» (He leaves without anyone seeing him) — English uses "-ing", Spanish needs a full subjunctive clause. With the same subject, use «sin» + infinitive: «Sale sin hacer ruido» (without making a noise). STEP 6: «¿para qué?» asks the purpose (What for?), while «¿por qué?» asks the cause (Why?). STEP 7: don't use the infinitive when someone ELSE does the action: «Te llamo para ayudarte» (I'm calling to help you — I help) vs «Te llamo para que me ayudes» (I'm calling so that you help me — you help).

PASSO 1: algumas conjunções de condição: STEP 1: some conjunctions of condition always take the subjunctive, because they talk about something that hasn't happened or may not happen: «con tal de que, a menos que, a no ser que, en caso de que, siempre que (= provided that)». STEP 2: examples: «Iremos al lago a menos que llueva» (We'll go to the lake unless it rains), «Te presto el coche con tal de que lo cuides» (I'll lend you the car as long as you look after it), «Llévate el paraguas en caso de que llueva» (Take the umbrella in case it rains). English uses the plain present after "unless", "in case", "as long as" — Spanish uses the subjunctive. STEP 3: «siempre que» has two meanings. As a condition (provided that), it takes the subjunctive: «Puedes venir siempre que avises». Meaning "whenever" (habit), it takes the indicative: «Siempre que llego, me saluda». STEP 4: «aunque» changes meaning with the mood — and English uses two different words for it. With the indicative, it's a known fact: «Aunque llueve, saldremos» (ALTHOUGH it's raining, we'll go out). With the subjunctive, it's a hypothesis or something that doesn't matter: «Aunque llueva, saldremos» (EVEN IF it rains, we'll go out). STEP 5: sum it up: if you know it and state it, indicative; if it's possible, future or irrelevant, subjunctive. STEP 6: after these conjunctions with a different subject, the infinitive doesn't exist: «a menos que» needs a conjugated verb.
o português usa subjuntivo nas mesmas co: English "unless it rains", "in case it rains", "as long as you look after it" use the plain present; Spanish uses the subjunctive: «a menos que llueva», «en caso de que llueva», «con tal de que lo cuides». And English "although" / "even if" are one Spanish word, «aunque»: indicative for "although" (a fact), subjunctive for "even if" (a hypothesis).
